about: The evangelium of the formulary “Third Sunday after Epiphany” in the 1962 Roman Missal.

seg.tr: At that time, when Jesus had come down from the mountain, great multitudes followed Him. And behold, a leper came and adored Him, saying: Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean. Jesus stretched out His hand, touched him, and said: I am willing; be made clean. Immediately his leprosy was cleansed. Jesus said to him: See that you tell no one; but go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift which Moses commanded, for a testimony to them. But when He had entered Capharnaum, a centurion came to Him, beseeching Him and saying: Lord, my servant lies at home paralyzed and is grievously tormented. Jesus said to him: I will come and heal him. The centurion said in reply: Lord, I am not worthy that You should enter under my roof; but only say the word, and my servant will be healed. For I also am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one: Go, and he goes; and to another: Come, and he comes; and to my servant: Do this, and he does it. Jesus, on hearing this, marveled and said to those who followed Him: Amen I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel. I say to you, however, that many will come from the East and the West and will sit down with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, but the children of the kingdom will be cast out into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Jesus said to the centurion: Go, and as you have believed, let it be done for you. And the servant was healed in that hour.

a.g: See that you tell no one
am a man placed under authority
On hearing this, however, Jesus marveled
but the children of the kingdom
let it be done for you

ex.w026: Here mundare is an active infinitive dependent on potes: “You can make me clean”. The identically spelt mundare after Volo is instead a second-person passive imperative: “Be made clean”.
ex.w035: Mundare is a second-person singular passive imperative addressed to the leper: “Be made clean”. It is not the active infinitive in the earlier potes me mundare.
ex.w040: Latin speaks of his leprosy being cleansed: mundata agrees with lepra. The cleansing concerns the previously mentioned leper. Leprosy remains the subject of the Latin sentence.
ex.w110: Verbo is an instrumental ablative: the healing is to be effected by a word alone. “Say the word” is the natural English request. It does not make the Latin noun accusative.
